rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the Torah reference continues the chain of testimony: Moses’ Book preceded the Qur’an as an imām and mercy, while Jesus’ testimony was mentioned first for special reasons.
rows.anchor: the testimony of Jesus (sws) was mentioned first. This reference of the Torah expresses the continuity of the testimony

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imām means guide; the Book guides in this world and becomes mercy in the next, so people must obey its worldly directives rather than merely honor or kiss it.
rows.anchor: The word imām means “guide.” This is exactly the same thing as has been stated about the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an confirms the Torah by fulfilling Moses’ predictions about it, not simply by affirming the Torah’s divine status.
rows.anchor: a materialization of these predictions and in this manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the common argument that the Qur’an is divine merely because it recognizes the Torah as divine; only fulfilled predictions in the Torah can testify to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: Generally, people have interpreted this verse to mean that since Qur’ ān accepts the Torah as a divine book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an regards earlier scriptures as divine yet corrupted, so its attestation is limited to fulfilled predictions; taṣdīq commonly has this specific Arabic sense.
rows.anchor: regards these scriptures to be divine but at the same time declares them to be inflicted with corruptions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revelation in Arabic honored the language, chose Arabs to convey and witness to religion, and removed their excuse to deny the truth; the Torah predicts the final Messenger would be an unlettered Ishmaelite.
rows.anchor: God by revealing the Qur’ān in Arabic enhanced the respect commanded by the language, lent it the sanction of eternal existence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s attentive response and mission to reform their people show that the Qur’an and its Messenger are not at fault when the intended human audience rejects them; their own crookedness is to blame.
rows.anchor: The blame does not lie on the Book or on him; it is their own crooked nature which is responsible for their aversion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes by warning the disbelievers and urging the Prophet to meet their rejection with patience and forbearance.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers are warned and threatened and the Prophet (sws) is urged to show patience and forbearance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn overheard the Qur’an by chance through God’s sudden direction; neither the Prophet arranged the encounter nor had the jinn intended to listen.
rows.anchor: the incident of the jinn overhearing the Qur’ ān was a chance happening ordained by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reports that the encounter occurred at Nakhlah on the Prophet’s return from Ṭā’if, when jinn chanced upon his night recitation as he prayed while dejected.
rows.anchor: this incident took place when the Prophet (sws) reached Nakhlah to spend a night there on his way back from Ṭā’if

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s fervent advocacy contrasts with Quraysh and Ṭā’if’s mistreatment of the Messenger; this shows the fault lies in people who evade the Qur’an, not in it or its bearer.
rows.anchor: the upright among the jinn who accidentally heard a few of its verses were so stirred by it that they became its fervent proponents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn immediately signaled their companions to listen respectfully, a contrast with Makkan opponents who taught others to make noise and drown out Qur’anic recitation.
rows.anchor: they beckoned their companions to silently and respectfully hear these divine words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The citation from Sūrah al-Jinn describes listeners rushing toward the Prophet as he invokes God, reinforcing the jinn’s eager response to the recitation.
rows.anchor: it seems as if they will rush upon him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn did more than praise the Qur’an: they warned their people and boldly proclaimed it despite danger; praise matters when it changes practical conduct.
rows.anchor: they did not stop at merely praising and lauding its words; they embarked upon a campaign

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn introduce the Qur’an as a Book revealed after Moses in confirmation of earlier scriptural predictions; after Moses, only Muhammad brought a new sharī‘ah, while Israelite prophets followed Mosaic law.
rows.anchor: after Moses (sws), it is only Mu ḥammad who as a Messenger gave a new sharī‘ah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah was the principal divine Book before the Qur’an and other scriptures supplemented it; the Qur’an is the independent Book after it, with fulfilled predictions as its strongest proof of divine origin.
rows.anchor: After the Torah, it was the Qur’ ān that can be regarded as an independent Book

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparing the jinn’s description here with Sūrah al-Jinn clarifies that the Qur’an guides to monotheism and the straight path.
rows.anchor: By comparing both these, it is evident that the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq denotes monotheism, the straight path to God, a firmly grounded belief aligned with reality, reason, and human nature; ṣirāṭ mustaqīm is easy, level, and free of deviation, with indefiniteness expressing grandeur.
rows.anchor: that leads a person to God. It also refers to the firmly established and firmly grounded nature of this belief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s central demand is that their people answer God’s summoner and believe; the imperative stresses that faith is the required response, which brings forgiveness and rescue from painful doom.
rows.anchor: the real message is referred to which the jinn delivered to their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min in ‘forgive some of your sins’ is partitive, referring to grave violations of human rights that require restitution; if restitution is missed, justice requires the case be reopened at Judgment.
rows.anchor: It refers to those sins which are not forgiven even after professing faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failing to make amends when one can is contrary to faith; when amends are no longer possible, remorse, repentance, and later good deeds may intercede, though the final verdict is unknown.
rows.anchor: if a person does not atone for such sins in spite of having the opportunity, then this is against the requisites of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects treating min as surplus because the Qur’an has no redundant words, and warns that both baseless despair and baseless optimism about God can lead to trials.
rows.anchor: There is not a single surplus word in the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the warning could be read as God’s own addition, Islahi prefers reading the words about those who do not answer as part of the jinn’s speech, as in Sūrah al-Jinn.
rows.anchor: in my opinion in the light of parallel verses of the Qur’ ān, these words are from the jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning says that just as people cannot escape God in this world, they will have no helper against Him in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: just as they cannot escape God’s grasp in this world, in a similar manner, they will have no one to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s call to believe in Muhammad raises whether they are Qur’anic addressees and he is their Messenger in the same way as for humans.
rows.anchor: what is the meaning of statement given by the jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi argues that a messenger’s established mission requires being from the people, speaking their language, living among them, conclusively warning the whole society, then disavowing and migrating if they reject; the Prophet did not fulfill this course among jinn.
rows.anchor: messengers were members of the people they were sent to; they presented their message in their language and spent their lives among their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A human messenger cannot be a complete practical model for jinn, just as an angel or jinn could not model human life; the Qur’an answers why humans receive human messengers by saying an angel would appear as a human.
rows.anchor: Can the life of a human be a complete example for the jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because humans and jinn arise from conflicting substances, their temperaments and needs differ; common guidance can concern monotheism, the Hereafter, and moral principles, while other directives require messengers from among jinn.
rows.anchor: when the jinn and humankind have been created from two conflicting substances, it is essential

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Jinn says the Prophet learned the jinn’s impressions by revelation; if he were their Messenger, Islahi argues, he would know them directly and preach to them as he did to Arabia, which the Qur’an does not show.
rows.anchor: he would have directly known these impressions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports of jinn delegations or the Prophet visiting them are discrepant and need scrutiny; even if true, occasional meetings would not discharge a Messenger’s full duty toward them.
rows.anchor: there is such discrepancy in these narratives that they need to be evaluated with respect to their texts as well as chains of narration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religious fundamentals are shared across humans, jinn, angels, and the wider universe; like birds and mountains joining David’s praise, righteous jinn praised the Qur’an and urged belief in monotheism, resurrection, and fear of punishment.
rows.anchor: the broader principles of religion are concerned, they are totally common between mankind and jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s basic message applies to humans and jinn, but Muhammad is not their Messenger in the same manner as he is to humans; that claim conflicts with God’s stated practice of messengership.
rows.anchor: it would not be right to say that Muḥammad (sws) is a messenger to the jinn in the same manner he is to mankind

rows.speaker: Imām Abū Ḥanīfah
rows.claim: Abū Ḥanīfah is reported to have withheld or been cautious about explicitly saying righteous jinn enter Paradise, since these verses promise them only deliverance from torment.
rows.anchor: it is attributed to Imām Abū Ḥanīfah that he was not of the view that the righteous jinn would enter Paradise

rows.speaker: later scholars
rows.claim: Later scholars defend Abū Ḥanīfah’s position by arguing that even if the righteous are not admitted, this would not violate justice.
rows.anchor: in spite of a person’s piety and righteousness, He does not admit him into Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi objects to denying righteous jinn Paradise: if evil jinn must go to Hell, he asks why the righteous should be deprived of Paradise.
rows.anchor: When the evil among the jinn will necessarily go to Hell, why should their righteous be deprived of Paradise?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse warns deniers by asking whether the God who created heaven and earth effortlessly can raise the dead; Islahi links this to other Qur’anic arguments for resurrection.
rows.anchor: the God Who created the heavens and the earth without any bother is capable of raising the dead to life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an also asks whether creating heaven and earth or restoring the dead is harder; God answers that the Creator of the first has power over everything.
rows.anchor: God, Who was not unable to create the heavens and the earth not only has the power to resurrect the dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When its audience is cornered and cannot answer, the Qur’an sometimes supplies the answer itself; Islahi sees this pattern in the verse’s closing affirmation.
rows.anchor: when the Qur’ān’s addressees are so cornered that at times they are unable to answer a question posed, the Qur’ān itself puts forth the answer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning continues with disbelievers before Hell admitting the Judgment is real, then being told to taste torment for their disbelief.
rows.anchor: After this confession from them, they will be told to taste torment in retribution of their disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evidence for the Hereafter is plain within humans and in the world around them; deniers reject it without sound reason because they refuse to sacrifice base desires.
rows.anchor: the arguments which substantiate the Hereafter are so evident in the world within man and the one outside him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People deny resurrection because they will not sacrifice their desires; those who set appetite above intellect, human nature, and the testimony of messengers do not merit leniency.
rows.anchor: people who in merely following their whims and desires have denied their own intellect, their nature and then all prophets and messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must persevere like all earlier messengers, each of whom passed every trial; min in ‘the messengers’ is explanatory and inclusive, not partitive.
rows.anchor: All prophets of God faced trials one greater than the other and all of them without exception succeeded one hundred percent in these trials

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command not to hurry concerns opponents who taunt the Prophet by demanding punishment; when it arrives, their present respite will seem only an hour or day.
rows.anchor: if these people are trying to irk the Prophet (sws) by asking him to hasten the punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Balāgh is the predicate of an omitted subject, emphasizing that the Prophet’s duty is to deliver the warning fully and leave no excuse for denial; the punishment’s victims bear responsibility.
rows.anchor: The implication is that the Prophet’s duty is to only deliver his warnings fully

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the sixth group of seventeen sūrahs: its first seven are Makkan and its remaining ten are Madinan; Islahi rejects the report that Sūrah al-Raḥmān is Madinan.
rows.anchor: With this sūrah begins the sixth group. Altogether there are seventeen sūrahs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Resurrection is the group’s central theme, with other Qur’anic topics subordinated to it; the Medinan sūrahs also spell out the obedience that faith in resurrection requires.
rows.anchor: The comprehensive central theme of this whole group is resurrection on the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Makkan sūrahs primarily address Quraysh while comforting the Prophet and Muslims; the Medinan sūrahs address believers, hypocritical weaknesses, and the People of the Book who supported Quraysh.
rows.anchor: In the Makkan sūrahs, the debate is against the beliefs and notions of the disbelievers of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah Qāf’s central theme is proving life after death and accountability, answering Quraysh’s objection that decayed bodies cannot be recreated.
rows.anchor: The central theme of this sūrah is to substantiate life after death

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s grandeur proves its divine origin; calling it poetry or soothsaying is a pretext for denying resurrection, driven by pride and confusion, although God knows what earth consumes and records people’s deeds and words.
rows.anchor: The grandeur and magnificence of the Qur’ ān bear witness that it is the word of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heaven and earth provide signs for resurrection, reward and punishment, and monotheism by showing God’s power, wisdom, and provision; they warn the humble who turn to Him.
rows.anchor: A reference is made to the signs of the heavens and the earth which if benefited from bear evidence to the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are warned that earlier nations were destroyed for pride and arrogance, and their fate will be the same if they persist.
rows.anchor: Nations before them who were guilty of this crime were totally destroyed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge and creative power establish resurrection, and He has secured the record of human deeds and utterances.
rows.anchor: The Almighty’s attributes of Knowledge and Creativity which prove the certainty of the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage vividly depicts Judgment and contrasts the dreadful fate awaiting disbelievers with the good fate of believers.
rows.anchor: A vivid description of the Day of Judgement is drawn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh must not imagine its power and glory are lasting: stronger, more splendid nations were destroyed at their height and could not escape retribution; their histories teach the heedful.
rows.anchor: Many other nations, who had much more power and splendour were destroyed at the very height of their dominance and authority
